summary:
Astroverse is an interactive lunar astronaut mission training experience designed to introduce children to the science, technology and challenges of space exploration. Developed as a junior astronaut mission trainer, it transforms theoretical learning into hands on exploration through a simulated lunar environment, custom six wheeled rovers, interactive mission stations and five educational missions covering solar energy, life support systems, radiation protection, hydroponics and space weather.

By combining immersive gameplay with real world scientific concepts and NASA open science data integration, Astroverse allows young learners to explore the responsibilities and problem solving involved in sustaining human presence on the Moon. It addresses the challenge by making astronaut training concepts accessible, engaging and experiential rather than purely instructional.

This project is important because it bridges the gap between curiosity and scientific understanding, encouraging the next generation to develop an interest in STEM, space technology and exploration. It aims to make young learners not just observers of humanity's journey into space, but active participants in imagining and understanding it.
details:
ASTROVERSE operates through an interconnected system of player controls, interactive objects, mission logic and environmental mechanics. Players can interact with different installations across the lunar base, trigger mission-specific events, receive instructions through the journal interface and track their progress.

The environment incorporates custom movement and physics configurations to reproduce aspects of lunar exploration. The rover, for instance, uses a six-wheel configuration with suspension mechanics to navigate uneven terrain. Mission interactions are managed through scripted events, while player progress is maintained through data persistence systems.

The project demonstrates how accessible game-development technology can be used to build complex, interactive simulations without requiring specialized hardware. Its modular mission architecture also allows additional scenarios, scientific challenges and interactive installations to be incorporated without rebuilding the entire experience. Integrating external scientific datasets introduces players to the idea that simulations can interact with real-world information rather than operate entirely on fictional scenarios.

Beyond its immediate educational application, ASTROVERSE explores the potential of interactive digital environments as accessible platforms for science communication. We intend for the project to serve as a foundation that can be expanded with more advanced mission scenarios, additional scientific datasets and increasingly sophisticated simulations.

The project was developed using the following technologies:

• Roblox Studio: Primary development environment for building the lunar terrain, structures, interactive installations and overall experience.

• Luau: Used for gameplay programming, mission scripting, player interactions, physics configurations and interface logic.

• Roblox Physics Engine: Used to implement rover movement, suspension, force-based mechanics and environmental physics.

• NASA CCMC DONKI API: Integrated through HTTP requests to retrieve relevant space-weather information.

• Roblox DataStoreService: Used for player progress persistence.

• Roblox GUI Framework: Used to develop the astronaut journal, mission interfaces, instructions and interactive displays.

• Git and GitHub: Used for source-code management, project organisation and collaborative development.

The project was developed as a software-based experience without requiring specialized external hardware.

One of our central design decisions was to avoid relying on conventional game interfaces. We developed a journal-inspired interaction system that draws from the visual language of astronaut field notes and mission documentation. The rover mechanics were also designed to go beyond basic vehicle movement, incorporating suspension behaviour and recovery systems to make navigation more engaging. Environmental design, interactive installations and mission-specific interfaces were developed to give different areas of the experience their own functional identity. Additionally, the inclusion of historical lunar exploration references creates a connection between simulated exploration and real human achievements.

During development, we prioritised the following factors:

• Performance optimization: Ensuring that environmental assets, scripts and physics systems remain manageable across different devices.

• Modularity: Structuring missions and interactive components so that individual features can be modified or expanded independently.

• Reliability: Accounting for external API failures through fallback mechanisms and ensuring that essential gameplay does not depend entirely on internet-based data retrieval.

• Physics consistency: Balancing realistic movement behaviour with the limitations of the game engine and the need for responsive controls.

• Interface usability: Designing readable, intuitive interfaces suitable for the intended age group.

• Scalability: Keeping the underlying architecture adaptable for future missions, additional datasets and more complex simulations.

The development process involved balancing scientific authenticity, technical feasibility, accessibility and an engaging user experience.
